attempts.raw_response: The particle velocity should not be confused with the speed of the wave itself, which describes how quickly the disturbance propagates through the medium. While the wave speed depends on the elastic and inertial properties of the medium, particle velocity refers to the localized motion of individual particles oscillating about their equilibrium positions. For a harmonic sound wave, the particle velocity is proportional to the acoustic pressure and inversely related to the characteristic acoustic impedance of the medium. This relationship is fundamental to understanding how energy is transported through acoustic systems. In fluids, particle velocity is typically aligned with the direction of wave propagation, whereas in solids, particles may move in various directions depending on the wave type.

pair.human_continuation:
When applied to a sound wave through a medium of a fluid like air, particle velocity would be the physical speed of a parcel of fluid as it moves back and forth in the direction the sound wave is travelling as it passes.

Particle velocity should not be confused with the speed of the wave as it passes through the medium, i.e. in the case of a sound wave, particle velocity is not the same as the speed of sound. The wave moves relatively fast, while the particles oscillate around their original position with a relatively small particle velocity. Particle velocity should also not be confused with the velocity of individual molecules, which depends mostly on the temperature and molecular mass.
pair.prefix: Particle velocity (denoted  or ) is the velocity of a particle (real or imagined) in a medium as it transmits a wave. The SI unit of particle velocity is the metre per second (m/s). In many cases this is a longitudinal wave of pressure as with sound, but it can also be a transverse wave as with the vibration of a taut string.
